title: How the Dirty Set Moves: Characterizing Schedule Reuse in Incremental Sparse Matrix Multiplication
summary: Sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, are central to scientific simulation, graph analytics and machine learning, and their multiplication with dense inputs is a core parallel kernel. In many applications the matrix stays fixed while only a few input rows change per step, so the result can be updated from those rows alone, which we call the dirty set. Sparse kernels often add a second optimization based on the inspector-executor principle, in which a tiled schedule is prepared once and reused across calls. However, when this reuse remains profitable as the dirty set moves is not well characterized. In this paper, we show that retained tiled execution rarely beats direct CSC in incremental sparse matrix multiplication, although incremental execution itself remains highly profitable. Across 21 SuiteSparse matrices and controlled patterns of motion, a direct column-wise incremental update is 2.1-8.2x faster than the best of eight full-recomputation codes, among them Intel oneMKL and PyTorch. Yet the same direct update outperforms a tiled executor that retains tile preparation and caches assembled schedules in 779 of 837 workloads. Separating reuse into per-tile preparation and cached schedules shows that the benefit comes from preparation; extra cache capacity seldom helps because a tile set rarely returns after a different one has intervened. Tiling is faster only when tiles merge many entries into each output write, a structural property that we predicted before measurement and confirmed on four held-out matrices of the same family. These results show that the structure of the matrix and the motion of the dirty set, rather than the sophistication of the schedule, determine whether reuse is profitable. We anticipate that our methodology and guidelines will help developers decide when to build schedule reuse into incremental sparse runtimes.

title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.

title: Parallel Sparse Outputs for Tensor Compilers
summary:
Sparse tensor compilers are commonly used high-performance tools that optimize tensor algebra programs over notoriously complex sparse data structures. Despite the ever-increasing size and scale of sparse datasets, there exists astonishingly little research on developing a parallel sparse tensor compiler. Existing approaches fail to parallelize or make assumptions about access patterns or output formats that limit generality.
  This paper presents Birdseed, the first tensor compiler to support all loop orderings over any standard sparse format in parallel. More specifically, Birdseed supports parallel sparse scatters and directly writes into list, bytemap, hash, and dense levels of fibertree sparse formats. Our approach exhibits asymptotic memory and time improvements over all previous work. We additionally demonstrate empirical speedups on challenging kernels to parallelize, such as histogram construction and SpMSpV.

title: Tracing Knowledge Lineage for Federated Unlearning under Mutual Distillation
summary: An edge server and nearby devices can train language models of different sizes together by mutual distillation. Federated unlearning (FU) and unlearning for large language models (LLMs) execute a removal request on one model. Under mutual distillation, however, the effect of the removed data has been copied into many students, and their uploads teach it back to the corrected teacher. We propose Holder-level Erasure via Replication-weighted Delta-closure (HERD), which decides which holders must be corrected. HERD records a knowledge lineage graph from the transfers that the server already performs and weights each edge by its transfer type. It computes how many times the residual at each holder will be copied and selects the cheapest set of holders whose correction bounds the cumulative residual after the request. A transfer guard and a rejoin rule cover the holders left uncorrected or offline. We prove that partial correction suffices only when the copy number of the lineage graph is below one, that averaging alone never reaches one, and that the correction set remains valid under link outages. On TOFU, HERD leaves 18% to 52% less cumulative residual than the strongest baseline at 6% to 12% of its correction cost.

title: The Cost of Context: Profiling the Energy Footprint of Input Tokens in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at HotCarbon'26, the 5th Workshop on Sustainable Computer Systems; to appear in ACM SIGENERGY Energy Informatics Review, Vol. 6, Issue 2
summary: The rapid adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context LLMs has shifted the computational burden toward the prefill phase---the initial stage where the model processes all input tokens in parallel before generating a response---yet its energy impact remains poorly characterised. We investigate the contradiction between massive hardware-level power spikes and the sub-linear marginal cost of input tokens reported in system-level studies. Through high-resolution telemetry of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2 models on NVIDIA A100 hardware, we identify the efficiency threshold where $O(n^2)$ attention complexity overcomes GPU parallelisation. Our results quantify how optimised memory orchestration (PagedAttention) delays this scaling bottleneck across three orders of context scaling, yielding up to an 8.9$\times$ energy efficiency advantage at 112,000 tokens compared to standard baselines. Furthermore, we characterise the energy disparity between input and output tokens, demonstrating that optimised serving (vLLM) causes this ratio to narrow (from $\approx$850$\times$ to 750$\times$) as context scales due to high decode efficiency, whereas unoptimised baselines show a much smaller, roughly constant gap ($\approx$150--230$\times$) because their prefill is itself expensive. This work establishes context-scaling laws that differentiate engine-level optimisations from inherent model constraints, providing an empirical framework for sustainable LLM deployment.

title: Bounding Mobile Latency from Network Interconnections
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, This paper is going to be published at the 21st Asian Internet Engineering Conference (AINTEC) in 2026 in Taipei, Taiwan
summary: Mobile latency is determined by how Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) route traffic: from phones, across the MNO's network to exit points where it enters the public Internet. Exit points are few, and MNOs are quiet about details, but their role prompts us to ask: What is the latency cost of sending traffic through an exit point? We develop a new method to evaluate this question, and demonstrate it on the three largest U.S. MNOs, although in principle it can apply globally. Using new analysis of existing traceroutes, we find that AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon funnel nationwide traffic through only 9, 5, and 9 exits, and the geographic detour they incur adds up to 62.1 ms compared to an ideal, direct-path latency. Routing delays also add latency. We show that even assuming speed-of-light paths through the exit points, latency is still up to 46.9 ms more than optimal. To understand if these costs can be overcome, we compare actual to theoretically optimal placements, finding that the latencies of current placements are 18-66% above the population-weighted optimum and 32-72% above the market-share-weighted optimum with the same number of exits. However, we show this gap is small in absolute terms: perfect placement would recover only a few milliseconds of the tens that remain. We show that geographic optimization saves little latency: the inflation users experience comes from routing and other overhead.

title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
summary: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.

title: Memento: Communicating Sensor Observations Through Shared Memory
summary: Wireless sensing systems often transmit highly redundant observations, making communication a bottleneck for low-power devices. We present Memento, a communication system that exploits recurring content by transmitting observations by reference. The sender embeds each observation and searches a shared vector table stored in persistent memory. When it finds a sufficiently similar prior observation, it sends a compact reference; otherwise, it sends the observation itself and adds it to the table. This design shifts work from wireless communication to local computation and storage, without requiring a fixed task-specific model. We implement Memento on a microcontroller with an SD card and evaluate it on three image datasets and one radar dataset. Memento provides favorable accuracy-communication and accuracy-energy tradeoffs against compression-based and task-oriented baselines. At high-accuracy operating points, it matches cloud classification accuracy on three workloads while using 5.5 to 27.1 times less energy, and comes within 0.14 percentage points on a fourth while using 14.7 times less energy. These results show that retrieval over persistent local memory can reduce communication costs in recurrent sensing workloads.

title: TrimSO(2): Fast and Memory-Efficient Training of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
summary: Equivariant interatomic potentials enable accurate and efficient simulations of molecules and materials. Among them, models based on SO(2) convolutions reduce the cost of tensor products and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, but their training remains time-consuming and memory-intensive. Existing training implementations materialize large edge tensors for representation transformations surrounding dense matrix multiplications, increasing memory usage and data movement. We observe that these transformations can be integrated into the model's existing dataflow, avoiding separate intermediate materialization. We introduce TrimSO(2), a fast and memory-efficient algorithm for SO(2)-based equivariant models. It realizes this principle through rotation on gather, recombination with activation, and inverse rotation on reduction, with support for the higher-order differentiation required for training. By avoiding intermediate materialization, TrimSO(2) delivers 2.71-16.73$\times$ operator speedups across forward, backward, and double backward and reduces model-level high-bandwidth memory traffic by 3.81-9.88$\times$. Finally, TrimSO(2) achieves 2.07-2.94$\times$ training speedups and 1.53-3.16$\times$ reductions in peak training memory over PyTorch implementations for official eSEN, UMA, and EquiformerV3 workloads on A100 and H100 GPUs.

title: BIER-DC: Stateless Multicast for In-Orbit Space Data Centers in LEO Constellations
summary: Emerging data-intensive space applications generate large volumes of data that must be processed, stored, replicated, and delivered efficiently. However, relying on terrestrial cloud regions can expose satellite data to high delivery latency and loss of timeliness due to intermittent satellite-to-ground visibility and limited access to ground infrastructure. Space Data Centers (SDCs), which organize collaborative satellites into logical compute and storage clusters, offer a promising approach for in-orbit data management and service continuity. In this paper, we first evaluate how satellite clustering with different sizes affects satellite visibility and gateway outage. We then propose BIER-DC, a stateless one-to-many communication protocol tailored for satellite-based SDCs. Unlike terrestrial multicast protocols designed for stable data center fabrics, BIER-DC decouples inter-SDC forwarding from intra-SDC delivery and encodes compact cluster-level forwarding information in packet headers. Comparative evaluations against BIER, BIER-TE, and Yeti show that BIER-DC significantly reduces packet-header length and byte-hop overhead, improving effective goodput and scalability for next-generation LEO space data centers.

title: Understanding NVIDIA Grace-Blackwell Unified Memory Through Placement-Controlled Microbenchmarks
summary:
NVIDIA Grace--Blackwell systems make CPU--GPU memory increasingly unified at the programming level, but unified addressability does not make the memory system uniform. A CUDA managed allocation on GB200 may be served from GPU-local HBM, accessed through host/system memory, demand-migrated, prefetched, reused after GPU access, or evicted and reloaded under capacity pressure. The problem is that these states share a programming interface while exercising different hardware paths and runtime mechanisms, making a single ``Unified Memory bandwidth'' number misleading.
  This paper presents a placement-controlled microbenchmark study of CUDA Unified Memory on NVIDIA GB200, using GH200 as a Grace--Hopper baseline and GB10/DGX Spark as a validation platform. Our methodology separates local HBM access, host/system-memory access, explicit movement, managed first touch, prefetch, reuse, access-pattern sensitivity, oversubscription, and CPU--GPU handoff, then summarizes the observations with a measurement-calibrated model of compute, access, migration, eviction, synchronization, and handoff costs. On GB200, a 1~GB STREAM-style triad reaches 3963~GB/s from local HBM but 304~GB/s through host-mapped CPU/system memory; for a 256~MB streaming kernel, cold CPU-initialized managed memory reaches 14.1~GB/s, while managed prefetch and reuse reach 4606~GB/s and 4504~GB/s. Below the capacity boundary, prefetched and reused managed memory remain above 4.6~TB/s, but at 125\% of CUDA-visible memory they fall to 968~GB/s and 1214~GB/s, showing that Grace--Blackwell unified memory must be understood through placement, access history, locality, reuse, and capacity pressure.

title: An Experimental Study on the Functional Correctness of Network Device Configurations Produced by Large Language Models
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2026 IEEE International Conference on Industry 4.0, Artificial Intelligence, and Communications Technology (IAICT)
summary: This paper presents a preliminary study on the efficacy of network device configuration produced by Large Language Models (LLMs). Currently, the study focuses on routing protocol configurations in a predefined small internetwork with Cisco-based routing devices. The capability of three freely available LLMs with standard capabilities (i.e., with no enhanced features) to produce effective setups is investigated. Prompt engineering methods are excluded in order to assess the "first-response" configurations of the models under consideration. The assessment method is based on the contents of the resulting routing table, aiming at measuring the device functional correctness. For that purpose, the Jaccard index is used to indicate the percentage of correct network prefixes contained in the routing table constructed by the model-based configuration commands. The work provides insights on the maturity and limitations of modern LLMs on aiding network administrators with network device configurations in real deployments.

title: CacheSmith: Accurate RAG Serving under Latency SLOs with Adaptive KV Reuse
summary: This paper presents CacheSmith, a KV cache reuse system for RAG prefill that maximizes quality-gated SLO attainment. While context caching lowers prefill latency by reusing precomputed KV states for retrieved chunks, it misses cross-chunk attention that a full prefill would compute over concatenated inputs. Prior selective recomputation schemes tackle this problem but enforce static, one-size-fits-all configurations that fail to effectively handle request heterogeneity or dynamic latency budgets. CacheSmith decomposes selective recomputation into a three-phase workflow of WarmUp, Probe, and Patch that can be dynamically configured to exploit a wide range of cost-accuracy trade-offs. At serving time, an SLO-aware scheduler in CacheSmith forms batches to mitigate inter-request interference during layer-by-layer prefill, while a budget-aware planner configures recomputation phases across the batch to maximize the number of requests satisfying both generation quality and latency targets. Both components make fast, solver-free decisions over profiled cost-accuracy bands. On four benchmarks across varying arrival rates and burstiness levels, CacheSmith improves quality-gated SLO attainment by up to 27.5%, over four state-of-the-art baselines.

title: SPARC: Substation-to-Peering Assessment of Resilience and Cascades
summary: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) operate from colocation facilities that draw power from regional grids and store limited backup fuel. In April 2025, the Iberian blackout kept the Spanish grid down for 16 hours, beyond the 12 hours of fuel required by the industry standard, while traffic at major Iberian IXPs fell by up to 70%. Yet operators cannot tell which facilities a grid event cuts off, whether it outlasts their backup, or where traffic from a failed IXP goes. We present SPARC, which maps power-grid and Internet dependencies from substations to IXPs and their traffic. Using open data validated against transmission operators, SPARC links 552 facilities hosting 275 IXPs to the substations that likely feed them. We spread grid events over this map and measure failover through controlled BGP withdrawals on the PEERING testbed. Disabling the most-shared 16% of facility-feeding substations cuts power to half of all IXP presences (an IXP at one facility), under half of what randomized maps require. Losing the 5% most central substations cuts power to 0.1% of IXP presences directly but to 9-52% once the grid splits into disconnected islands. Traffic often fails over to nearby sites that share the failing grid: a cascade affecting four metropolitan areas sends up to 40% of one area's monitored addresses to another of the four. We introduce SPARC-Shield to select substations to harden or facilities whose backup to extend. Against an attacker disabling ten substations, hardening the ten selected by SPARC-Shield reduces offline IXP presence by 72%, compared with 52% for the best standard ranking.

title: Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart Healthcare: Performance Comparison with an IP Baseline
summary: Smart healthcare IoT requires low-latency and reliable delivery of patient data, yet IP-based communication remains host-centric and offers limited support for mobility, caching, and request aggregation. This paper evaluates a smartphone-centric Named Data Networking (NDN) approach in which a patient's smartphone aggregates sensor streams and publishes a stable latest profile under a consistent name, enabling effective in-network caching. Using ndnSIM simulations on a realistic medical IoT topology, we compare NDN and IP under identical traffic and link conditions. Results show that per-sample naming provides little benefit, but smartphone aggregation with stable naming allows NDN caching to reduce delay after cache warm-up and achieve significantly higher delivery ratios under congestion compared to IP.

title: A Multiarmed Bandit Approach for LTE-U/Wi-Fi Coexistence in a Multicell Scenario
summary: Recent studies and literature reviews have shown promising results for 3GPP system solutions in unlicensed bands when coexisting with Wi-Fi, either by using the duty cycle (DC) approach or licensed-assisted access (LAA). However, it is widely known that general performance in these coexistence scenarios is dependent on traffic and how the duty cycle is adjusted. Most DC solutions configure their parameters statically, which can result in performance losses when the scenario experiences changes on the offered data. In our previous works, we demonstrated that reinforcement learning (RL) techniques can be used to adjust DC parameters. We showed that a Q-learning (QL) solution that adapts the LTE DC ratio to the transmitted data rate can maximize the Wi-Fi/LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U) aggregated throughput. In this paper, we extend our previous solution by implementing a simpler and more efficient algorithm based on multiarmed bandit (MAB) theory. We evaluate its performance and compare it with the previous one in different traffic scenarios. The results demonstrate that our new solution offers improved balance in throughput, providing similar results for LTE and Wi-Fi, while still showing a substantial system gain. Moreover, in one of the scenarios, our solution outperforms the previous approach by 6% in system throughput. In terms of user throughput, it achieves more than 100% gain for the users at the 10th percentile of performance, while the old solution only achieves a 10% gain.

title: Prioritizing Microservice Requests via Retries
summary:
Cloud services rapidly shift towards independently-managed microservices architectures. This independence may lead to temporary microservices miscoordination, resulting in overloads and rejections of valuable transactions. This weakness may further be exploited by attackers to launch overload attacks inflicting performance and cost damages.
  Retry operations are a key machinery aiming at overcoming seldom rejections. However, during overload periods they: a) Fail protecting valuable transactions from rejections, and b) Trigger large-scale performance-degrading retry storms.
  We propose simple modifications in retry operations, overcoming these deficiencies by transforming retries into a rejection prioritization mechanism, DiffTry (Differential Retries). It is based on a simple, lightweight, distributed and stateless design and requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination.
  We develop an analytical model capturing DiffTry's effectiveness for two services in tandem, then generalize it to networks of services. Our theoretical framework lets practitioners quantify, for a given network, the resulting prioritization and rejection rates, and yields formal guarantees that DiffTry substantially reduces the impact of both incidental and adversarial orchestrated overloads. We validate these predictions in simulation and on a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry is a simple drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application changes; the measured rejection closely matches the analysis.

title: Multi-Cell LTE-U/Wi-Fi Coexistence Evaluation Using a Reinforcement Learning Framework
summary: Cellular broadband Internet of Things (IoT) applications are expected to keep growing year-by-year, generating demands from high throughput services. Since some of these applications are deployed over licensed mobile networks, as long term evolution (LTE), one already common problem is faced: the scarcity of licensed spectrum to cope with the increasing demand for data rate. The LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U) forum, aiming to tackle this problem, proposed LTE-U to operate in the 5 GHz unlicensed spectrum. However, Wi-Fi is already the consolidated technology operating in this portion of the spectrum, besides the fact that new technologies for unlicensed band need mechanisms to promote fair coexistence with the legacy ones. In this work, we extend the literature by analyzing a multi-cell LTE-U/Wi-Fi coexistence scenario, with a high interference profile and data rates targeting a cellular broadband IoT deployment. Then, we propose a centralized, coordinated reinforcement learning framework to improve LTE-U/Wi-Fi aggregate data rates. The added value of the proposed solution is assessed by a ns-3 simulator, showing improvements not only in the overall system data rate but also in average user data rate, even with the high interference of a multi-cell environment.
